newsitem.title: FRANCE: SLOT MANAGEMENT TO BE KEY PROBLEM FOR EUROPEAN AVIATION.
newsitem.headline: SLOT MANAGEMENT TO BE KEY PROBLEM FOR EUROPEAN AVIATION.

text.p: Airport slot management and its impact on airport capacity will be one of the key problems for the European aviation industry in the next two years, said France's director-general of civil aviation, Pierre Graff.
He was addressing the annual conference of Airports Council International (ACI) Europe on Tuesday.

Separately, a leading expert on slot trading, Riga Doganis from Britain's Cranfield University, said the U.S. experience since 1986 "suggests secondary slot trading is possible and slots can be traded. But the more fundamental question is whether they should be".
Doganis is head of Cranfield's air transport department and was chairman of Greece's Olympic Airways between 1995-96.
He said: "It is less certain that slot trading will ensure any significant increase in airline competition on European routes currently operated as monopolies or duopolies."
There were two particular alternatives to slot trading which could be considered, Doganis added.
The first was the introduction at congested airports of peak period charges sufficiently high to clear excess demand for slots at peak periods.
The second was the auctioning by the airport authority of peak period slots for five- to seven-year periods.

"Neither of these will necessarily be any better than slot trading in ensuring increased opportunities for competition and new entrants. But they offer one major advantage for airports and governments. It is they who will collect the scarcity rent(value) from the provision of scarce runaway capacity rather than the airlines," Doganis added.

"The draft for an EU Council directive on airport charges is expected to be published soon and to propose that charges be cost-related. But (it) could be demand-related, where demand exceeds supply, in order to manage capacity more efficiently," he said.
"If this is the case, congested airports would be free to impose very high peak charges ," he added.
Copenhagen airport's chief executive, Niels Boserup told a press conference that ACI had proposed to the European Commission that airports should have a bigger say in slot reviews.
He also warned "that giant airline alliances will do everything to buy up slots and reduce competition which would be no benefit to customers".
"If slots are to be traded then there must be transparency," he stated"
